title: Rent From an Indian Flat Is Taxable in India, Treaty or NRE Account
excerpt: A Mint explainer walks through why Article 6 leaves India's right to tax Mumbai rent intact, why Article 25 relief comes as a US foreign tax credit, and why the account the rent lands in changes nothing.
body:
• No: neither the India-US tax treaty (DTAA) nor receiving rent in an NRE account makes rent from an Indian property tax-free in India, tax expert Harshal Bhuta explains in Mint.
  • Under Article 6 of the treaty, income from immovable property "may be taxed" in the country where the property sits — for a Mumbai flat, that is India, and paying US tax does not remove India's right to tax.
  • The treaty's relief works the other way: under Article 25, eligible Indian tax can be claimed as a foreign tax credit against US tax (claimed on Form 1116), subject to US rules and limits — the credit may not equal the full Indian tax paid.
  • Routing rent into an NRE account changes nothing about the rent's taxability; only the interest later earned on that NRE balance is a separate stream that may be exempt in India — and for a US tax resident it remains taxable in the US.

It is one of the most common questions Indian landlords in the United States ask: if the rent from a flat in India is already taxed in the US, can India tax it too — and would collecting the rent in an NRE account instead of an NRO account make it exempt? The short answer to both is no, as Harshal Bhuta, co-founder and country co-head for international tax and FEMA at Ascentium India, explains in a Mint explainer published on November 23. The question came from an Indian citizen living in the US — a US tax resident and a non-resident for Indian tax purposes — who owns a flat in Mumbai, earns rent from it, and reports that rent on his US return.

Article 6: the property's country taxes first

Under Article 6 of the India-US Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement, income from immovable property such as a house or flat "may be taxed" in the country where the property is situated, and that includes rental income. Because the flat is in Mumbai, India has the right to tax the rent under its domestic tax laws. The words "may be taxed" do not let the taxpayer choose where to pay, and paying tax in the US does not take away India's taxing right. Treaty guides make the same point in rate terms: for rent, the treaty sets no cap — normal Indian rates apply, with India taxing first.

Article 25: relief is a credit, not an exemption

As a US tax resident, the landlord is also liable to US tax on the same rent, because the US taxes residents on worldwide income. Article 25 of the treaty addresses that overlap: eligible Indian income tax can be claimed as a foreign tax credit against US income tax, subject to US tax laws and applicable limits — in practice, claimed on Form 1116. The treaty therefore ordinarily works through a credit in the US rather than an exemption in India, and the credit may not necessarily equal the full Indian tax paid, since its availability and amount depend on the applicable rules and limitations.

The account does not change the income

The second hope — that receiving rent in an NRE account makes it exempt — confuses two separate questions: whether a receipt may be credited to an account, and whether that receipt is taxable. Receiving rent in an NRE account does not change its nature or taxability under Indian income tax law; rent received in an NRE account remains rental income and is taxable accordingly. What is different is the interest subsequently earned on that balance: interest is a separate income stream and may qualify for exemption under the NRE-interest provisions in India. For a US tax resident, however, that exemption stops at the Indian border — NRE interest that is tax-free in India must still be reported and taxed in the US.

The practical sequence for a US-based landlord is therefore unchanged: the rent is taxable in India under Indian rules, the same rent is reported in the US, and the Indian tax actually paid is credited in the US within the treaty's and the IRS's limits. This article is general information on how the treaty works, not tax advice for any individual situation.
nri_angle: US-based NRIs renting out property in India get the treaty's actual mechanism — Indian tax first, US credit second — instead of the two most common misconceptions about it.
